paras: The lynching of Henry Young was the hanging of a Black tenant by a mob of about 100 men on the Bass plantation near Lake Cormorant, DeSoto County, Mississippi, on the night of August 16, 1905. Young, accused of killing the white plantation manager Edward E. Perry on Sunday, August 13, was taken from Sheriff Withers and a deputy at a railroad station. A Memphis account called the hanging quiet and orderly and said Black onlookers approved; the Oklahoma Safeguard, a Black paper, reprinted it and answered it in an editorial.

According to the Hernando Times-Promoter, the DeSoto County paper, Perry managed the plantation for E. L. Bass and Young was a tenant there. The first Memphis wire report called Perry "a well-known overseer" at Star Landing and a brother of Memphis police captain Oliver H. Perry.

In the Times-Promoter's version, Young had been drinking all Saturday night, shot his wife in a flesh wound, and fired on Perry "without warning" when Perry came to stop him. The first Memphis dispatch said Young had "become boisterous" and that Perry, wounded, drew a revolver as he fell and wounded his attacker. On August 15, with Young still at large, a Memphis item headed "Fruit For a Lynching" predicted it was "100 to 1 that he will be lynched."

Sheriff Withers hunted Young with a posse of forty and bloodhounds. Young was caught on the morning of August 16 trying to reach his father's home on an island; the Times-Promoter said a fisherman captured him near Penton. Withers and Deputy Scott brought him to a railroad station, Trenton in the wire report and Penton in the local paper and the New York Sun, to take a train to Hernando, the county seat. News of the capture spread, and the Times-Promoter wrote that "a crowd of determined citizens had formed for the purpose of lynching the prisoner."

While the officers waited for the train, about 100 armed men overpowered them and took Young. The mob carried him to the Bass plantation, where Perry had been shot, and hanged him from a tree. Wire reports said Young confessed but said he had not meant to kill Perry and that a pistol they were struggling over had gone off. According to the Times-Promoter, the mob dispersed as soon as Young was pronounced dead.
One brief report said the governor had offered a $200 reward for Young before his capture. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage.

The Commercial Appeal's special went out over the Associated Press wire and ran on August 17 and 18 from Birmingham and Montgomery to New York and Raleigh. Headlines were brief and alike: "Negro Hanged by Mississippi Mob" in the Birmingham Age-Herald, "Lynch Negro Slayer" in the New-York Tribune and "Negro Murderer Hung" in the Montgomery Advertiser. The pre-capture "Fruit For a Lynching" item ran in papers in Missouri, Arkansas and Mississippi.

The local Times-Promoter headlined its story "Murder and Lynching," called Young the murderer whose life "pays the penalty,". The New York Sun headed its fuller version "Missippi Mob Disposes of a Negro Murderer, Other Blacks Approving," stressing "no noise, no drinking, no firing of guns."

The only Black paper found to cover the case, the Oklahoma Safeguard, reprinted the Commercial Appeal account on August 24 under headlines calling it a "Quiet and Orderly Affair" by "One hundred Good Citizens." Beside it an editorial asked, if "the best citizens" had gone out lynching, "where is the Negro's hope for relief," and advised Black people to sell their possessions and move where they could "have the right to be tried." It rejected the claim that Black witnesses approved, saying that anyone there, "knowing those people as we do know them," would have done the same.

Accounts of the shooting differ: the Times-Promoter said Young fired without warning, while his reported confession called it an accident, and only the first Memphis dispatch, which placed it at Star Landing, said Perry wounded him. The Leader put the lynching on Tuesday night; the dated wire reports and the local paper place it on Wednesday, August 16.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Young
bases: A mob of about 100 men took Henry Young, accused of killing Edward E. Perry, from the sheriff and hanged him from a tree (A5, A16).

A mob of about 100 armed men overpowered Sheriff Withers and a deputy, took Young and hanged him, with no lawful authority (A5, A16); they acted as punishment for Perry's killing, a 'crowd of determined citizens' formed 'for the purpose of lynching the prisoner' (A16).
The local Hernando Times-Promoter (A15, A16) and the Commercial Appeal/AP wire (A5) independently agree on the capture, seizure from the sheriff and hanging on the Bass plantation.

accounts.label: Young's reported confession (wire)
accounts.gist: Young admitted the shooting but said he did not intend to kill Perry; the pistol they were struggling over went off.

accounts.label: Commercial Appeal / AP wire
accounts.gist: Captured fording a river to his father's cabin, taken from the sheriff at Trenton station by about 100 armed men and hanged on the Bass plantation; a quiet hanging approved by Black onlookers.

accounts.label: Black editor (Oklahoma Safeguard)
accounts.gist: Lynching by the 'best citizens' leaves Black people no one to appeal to; any Black approval at the scene was compelled by fear of the mob.

AP wire headlines 'Negro Hanged by Mississippi Mob', 'Lynch Negro Slayer', 'Negro Murderer Hung', with Young's plea of accident.
Pre-capture Memphis item 'Fruit For a Lynching' predicted lynching at 100 to 1.
Oklahoma Safeguard reprinted the 'Quiet and Orderly Affair' account and editorialized that 'the best citizens' lynching left no appeal, urging Black people to move away.
